notes.meaning: Naomi wanted to secure a peaceful and permanent home for Ruth through marriage. Ruth had faithfully stayed with her, and Naomi felt it was her duty as an elder to help her find security. Good parents and guardians naturally desire lasting rest and well-being for those in their care.

Naomi pointed out that Boaz was a close family relative, making him eligible to act as their family redeemer. She noted that he was winnowing barley that evening on the threshing floor, tossing grain into the breeze so the wind could blow away the light straw and chaff. Boaz would be staying overnight to guard his gathered harvest.

Naomi told Ruth to wash, put on sweet olive oil, dress in her best clothes, and go down quietly to the threshing floor. These preparations marked the end of Ruth's period of mourning and made her ready for a special meeting. Naomi wisely instructed her to wait out of sight until Boaz had finished his evening meal.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern commentators suggest that Ruth's washing and perfume were intended as an act of sexual seduction rather than an end to mourning.

notes.meaning: Naomi directed Ruth to watch where Boaz lay down to sleep after his meal. Once he was asleep, Ruth was to uncover his feet and lie down there in the humble posture of a servant waiting for directions. This act was an accepted, respectful way to awaken Boaz and ask him to act as her family protector.

Ruth promised to carry out everything her mother-in-law instructed. She trusted Naomi's wisdom and good character, knowing Naomi would not lead her into sin or disgrace. Her humble willingness to listen shows both her modesty and her faith.

Ruth went down from the town of Bethlehem to the threshing floor and carefully followed every instruction Naomi had given her. She did not act rashly or draw attention to herself. Her steady obedience proved her loyalty to her family.

Boaz ate, drank, and was cheerful and thankful for the harvest God had provided. He lay down to sleep by the grain heap to guard his crops against thieves during the lawless times of the judges. Ruth then crept in quietly, lifted the covering from his feet, and lay down across them.

Around midnight, Boaz woke up startled and turned to find someone lying at his feet in the dark. He was surprised because he had no prior knowledge of anyone coming to the threshing floor. Not knowing who was there, he felt around to understand what had disturbed his sleep.

When Boaz asked who was there, Ruth humbly introduced herself as his servant. She asked him to spread the corner of his garment over her, which was the customary way of asking him to marry and protect her. She based her bold request on the fact that he was a kinsman-redeemer, a relative who had the duty under God's law to protect the family name and property.

Boaz immediately spoke a blessing over Ruth instead of rebuking her. He praised her loyalty, noting that she chose to honour her late husband's family rather than chasing after younger men for money or romance. Her choice showed that she put duty and godliness ahead of selfish desires.

Boaz told Ruth not to be afraid and promised to do everything she asked. He explained that everyone in the town knew she was a woman of noble character and strong virtue. A good name and quiet faith earn true honour from others over time.

Boaz confirmed that he was indeed a family redeemer who had the right to help her. However, he honestly revealed that another man in Bethlehem was more closely related to Elimelech's family than he was. That relative had the first legal right under Israel's law to buy the land and marry Ruth.

Boaz told Ruth to rest safely where she was for the remainder of the night, since walking home in the dark would be dangerous. He made a solemn promise that if the closer relative refused to redeem her, he himself would do so without fail. Boaz showed great self-control and godly integrity by treating her with complete honor.

Ruth stayed resting at his feet until just before dawn and rose to leave while it was still too dark to recognize faces. Boaz was eager to protect both her good name and his own from unfair gossip. Godly people take great care to avoid even the appearance of wrongdoing.

Before Ruth left, Boaz had her hold open her large shawl and poured six generous measures of barley into it. This heavy gift was a substantial token of good faith, showing Naomi that he intended to resolve the situation right away. Boaz then returned to the city to take care of the legal business.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: A few modern writers have interpreted the barley gift as payment for sexual favors, though evangelical scholars strongly reject this reading as baseless and contrary to the text.

notes.meaning: When Ruth arrived home, Naomi eagerly asked her how her meeting had turned out. Ruth then recounted everything Boaz had said and done during the night. The good news brought great comfort and relief to Naomi's heart.

Ruth displayed the six measures of barley and explained that Boaz gave them so she would not return to Naomi empty-handed. This generous present showed his warm regard for Naomi as well as for Ruth. Boaz wanted Naomi to see that her years of bitter emptiness were coming to an end.

Naomi urged Ruth to wait quietly and patiently at home until they learned the final outcome. She assured Ruth that Boaz was a dependable man who would not rest until the whole matter was settled that very day. When believers have done what is right, they can rest in God's caring hands.
